learning.focus: Build a rich wine braise while protecting the meat from a hard boil.
learning.outcome: Tender beef and a smooth sauce made from all the Barolo and cooked vegetables.
before: Choose a whole shoulder piece suited to braising; ask for vena or cappello di prete if buying from an Italian butcher.
Plan the 12-hour refrigerator marinade and keep all of it for the sauce.
Use a heavy casserole with a close-fitting lid and enough room for the meat, wine and vegetables.
A removable food-safe spice sachet can hold the whole cloves and peppercorns during marinade and braising; keep the full quantities and remove it only after infusion.

checkpoints.cue: The dried beef develops a brown crust without blackened butter.
checkpoints.why: Surface moisture inhibits browning, and burned fat would carry through the wine sauce.

checkpoints.cue: The covered pot has occasional gentle bubbles, not a rolling boil.
checkpoints.why: Moderate heat limits evaporation while the tough cut gradually becomes tender.

checkpoints.cue: A fork or thin skewer enters the thickest part without resistance.
checkpoints.why: A safe minimum internal temperature is reached well before this braising cut becomes pleasantly tender.

checkpoints.cue: The blended sauce coats a spoon and the whole woody spices have been removed.
checkpoints.why: Reduction concentrates the wine and vegetables while removal leaves a smooth sauce.

troubleshooting.problem: The beef is safe but still tough.
troubleshooting.cause: The braising cut has not had enough time at gentle heat.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue covered cooking, checking the liquid and tenderness periodically; do not slice it merely because two hours have passed.

troubleshooting.problem: The sauce is too thin or sharply wine-forward.
troubleshooting.cause: The wine has not reduced enough after blending.
troubleshooting.fix: Keep the beef warm and simmer the sauce uncovered until it coats a spoon, stirring to prevent scorching. Do not assume the dish becomes alcohol-free.

learning.storage: Refrigerate in shallow containers within 2 hours, or within 1 hour above 90°F, and keep at 40°F or colder. Use within 3–4 days of the first cooking; reheating does not restart that clock. Reheat to 165°F throughout. Cool the beef in its sauce in shallow portions. Reheat covered and gently, adding a little water if the sauce has thickened. If storing the sauce separately as gravy, use it within 1–2 days.
learning.timing: The 12-hour marinade is followed by about 15–20 minutes of browning, 15 minutes with the vegetables, at least 2 hours of gentle braising, and a brief sauce finish while the meat rests. Plan 15–17 hours overall and more if tenderness requires it. Ingredient amounts scale, but roast thickness, pot fit and the number of pieces govern the cooking schedule; use additional casseroles rather than crowding or multiplying the time.

steps.title: Marinate overnight
steps.text: Pat the beef dry without rinsing it. Put {{ingredients}} in a covered, nonreactive container, arranging the vegetables and spices around the meat and pouring the wine over everything. Refrigerate at 40°F or colder for 12 hours, turning the meat once if the wine does not cover it.

steps.title: Brown the beef
steps.text: Lift out the beef and pat it dry. Drain the vegetables and spices, keeping all the wine marinade separately. Heat {{ingredients}} in a heavy casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the beef well on its broad sides, about 5 minutes per side, adjusting the heat so the butter does not burn. Choose a casserole that holds the roast snugly, can close with its lid and has room for all the wine and vegetables.

steps.title: Cook the vegetables and heat the marinade
steps.text: Add the drained vegetables and spices to the casserole. Cook for about 15 minutes, moving them around the beef so they soften without burning. Meanwhile, bring the reserved wine marinade to a full boil in a separate saucepan; it has been in contact with raw beef.

steps.title: Braise gently
steps.text: Have {{ingredients}} ready. Season the beef with salt, then pour all the boiled wine marinade into the casserole. Bring the liquid back to a simmer, cover and reduce the heat to maintain occasional gentle bubbles. Braise for at least 2 hours, turning the meat occasionally and checking that there is still liquid around it. Add a little hot water only if evaporation threatens to dry the pot. Continue until a fork or thin skewer enters the thickest part easily and the meat yields without resistance; a larger or tougher piece may take much longer. Whole beef must reach at least 145°F followed by a 3-minute rest, but this cut needs further cooking to become tender.

steps.title: Blend the wine sauce
steps.text: Lift the beef onto a warm board and rest it loosely covered while finishing the sauce, about 10 minutes. Remove and discard the bay leaves, rosemary stem, cinnamon, cloves and peppercorns from the pot. Blend the cooked vegetables and wine with an immersion blender until smooth, keeping the blade submerged. Return the sauce to the heat and boil gently for a few minutes, or until it coats a spoon. Adjust with {{ingredients}}.

steps.title: Slice and serve
steps.text: Slice the rested beef across the grain. Arrange it on a warm platter and spoon the hot wine sauce over it. Serve with polenta to catch the sauce.

exactAfter.body:
## Chef's Note

The Cuneo version keeps Barolo at the center of the dish, with rosemary, cloves and a little cinnamon warming the sauce. Keep the butter and oil for browning, then give the beef the gentle cooking it needs. Blending the vegetables into the wine makes a full sauce for the sliced meat and polenta.

## Directions

1. **Marinate overnight:** Pat the beef dry without rinsing it. Put boneless beef shoulder for braising, bottle of Barolo wine, carrots, celery ribs, onion, rosemary sprig, whole cloves, garlic clove, bay leaves, black peppercorns, and small piece of cinnamon stick in a covered, nonreactive container, arranging the vegetables and spices around the meat and pouring the wine over everything. Refrigerate at 40°F or colder for 12 hours, turning the meat once if the wine does not cover it.
2. **Brown the beef:** Lift out the beef and pat it dry. Drain the vegetables and spices, keeping all the wine marinade separately. Heat butter and olive oil in a heavy casserole over medium-high heat. Brown the beef well on its broad sides, about 5 minutes per side, adjusting the heat so the butter does not burn. Choose a casserole that holds the roast snugly, can close with its lid and has room for all the wine and vegetables.
3. **Cook the vegetables and heat the marinade:** Add the drained vegetables and spices to the casserole. Cook for about 15 minutes, moving them around the beef so they soften without burning. Meanwhile, bring the reserved wine marinade to a full boil in a separate saucepan; it has been in contact with raw beef.
4. **Braise gently:** Have salt and hot water ready. Season the beef with salt, then pour all the boiled wine marinade into the casserole. Bring the liquid back to a simmer, cover and reduce the heat to maintain occasional gentle bubbles. Braise for at least 2 hours, turning the meat occasionally and checking that there is still liquid around it. Add a little hot water only if evaporation threatens to dry the pot. Continue until a fork or thin skewer enters the thickest part easily and the meat yields without resistance; a larger or tougher piece may take much longer. Whole beef must reach at least 145°F followed by a 3-minute rest, but this cut needs further cooking to become tender.
5. **Blend the wine sauce:** Lift the beef onto a warm board and rest it loosely covered while finishing the sauce, about 10 minutes. Remove and discard the bay leaves, rosemary stem, cinnamon, cloves and peppercorns from the pot. Blend the cooked vegetables and wine with an immersion blender until smooth, keeping the blade submerged. Return the sauce to the heat and boil gently for a few minutes, or until it coats a spoon. Adjust with salt.
6. **Slice and serve:** Slice the rested beef across the grain. Arrange it on a warm platter and spoon the hot wine sauce over it. Serve with polenta to catch the sauce.

wholeRecipeReview.allocations: All beef, bottle of wine, vegetables and spices assigned to marinade and carried through sear/braise/sauce. All 40 g butter and 3–4 tbsp oil to sear. Separate unmeasured salt allowances at braise and sauce finish. Whole woody/aromatic solids infuse then are discarded, vegetables and garlic blended. Hot-water evaporation replacement is listed and conditional; no added broth.
wholeRecipeReview.ratios: 1 kg beef for six portions is about 167 g raw beef per source portion, with sides appropriate. Wine remains one source bottle without invented milliliters or bottle-strength conversion. Full fat allocation retained; no tested cooked yield or alcohol-removal percentage.
wholeRecipeReview.capacity: Whole braising shoulder, snug heavy lidded casserole able to hold roast plus full wine/vegetable load and allow turning; larger batch may require additional casseroles. No exact pot size or promised liquid coverage.
wholeRecipeReview.ingredientState: Boneless whole braising shoulder translation of source cuts, patted dry not washed; coarse vegetable pieces; whole spices; Barolo preserved. Olive oil selects a conventional oil without altering source amount.
wholeRecipeReview.heatDoneness: Brown broad sides without burning butter. Full boil raw-contact wine before reuse. Occasional gentle bubbles under lid, at least 2 hours then fork/skewer tenderness. Whole-beef 145°F plus 3-minute minimum is distinguished from higher/longer tenderness endpoint; no invented target such as 195°F.
wholeRecipeReview.schedule: 12-hour refrigerated marinade, roughly 15–20-minute sear, 15-minute vegetable stage, >=2-hour braise, sauce while ~10-minute rest overlaps. 15–17 hours planning, longer if tough.
wholeRecipeReview.storage: Cool beef in sauce shallow/rapid, 3–4-day refrigerator window and 165°F reheat. Separately stored gravy uses stricter 1–2-day guidance.
